lessons.title: How to read a compliance page
lessons.summary: This lesson is educational. It is not legal advice, not a compliance opinion, and not a filing. Statutes and the FCC pages outrank this lab. A quiz answer is not a legal conclusion.
objectives: Treat this track as study material
Prefer the statute or the agency page over a paraphrase
Separate SIP headers from messaging rules

illustration.title: What outranks this page
illustration.caption: If a sentence here and the statute disagree, the statute wins. This lab is not a lawyer.

layers.name: Statute or rule

paragraphs: This lesson is educational. It is not legal advice, not a compliance opinion, and not a filing. Nothing in this track tells you that your system is lawful, that a certificate is valid, or that a campaign is approved. Those are decisions for the texts and for counsel.

When this lab names a date or a duty, it is repeating a sentence from a page that was opened. The sources block at the bottom is the check. If a link says confirm, this environment could not open it, and you should open it yourself before you rely on it.

STIR is a SIP identity mechanism. The Identity header and PASSporT are specified in RFC 8224 and RFC 8225. SHAKEN is the telephone-industry application described on the ATIS STI-GA page. 10DLC, on The Campaign Registry site, is an application-to-person messaging channel. It is not a SIP method and it does not authenticate a voice call.

Emergency calling has its own documents: RFC 6881 is a best current practice, RFC 6442 conveys location in SIP, and the statutes below are United States public laws about multi-line telephone systems. A working INVITE does not prove any of those duties are met.

lessons.title: STIR and SHAKEN
lessons.summary: RFC 8224 defines a signed SIP Identity header. RFC 8225 defines PASSporT. SHAKEN is the industry mechanism the ATIS STI-GA page describes. Educational only.
objectives: Repeat the FCC description without treating this page as the rule

illustration.title: Sign, then verify
illustration.caption: The protocol pieces are IETF documents. The governance body on the page this lab opened is the STI-GA.

states.name: PASSporT
states.detail: RFC 8225. A signed token about the originator.

states.name: Identity
states.detail: RFC 8224. The SIP header that carries the signature.

states.name: SHAKEN
states.detail: ATIS-SIP Forum mechanism, described by the STI-GA.

paragraphs: RFC 8224 says the baseline SIP security mechanisms are inadequate to assure the identity of the end users that originate SIP requests, especially between domains. It defines a SIP header field that conveys a signature used to validate the identity of the originator. It obsoletes RFC 4474.

RFC 8225 defines PASSporT, a Personal Assertion Token. The token is cryptographically signed to protect the integrity of the originator's identity and to let the destination verify that assertion. The abstract says the signature is intended to verify the originating persona even when it is sent over an insecure channel. PASSporT is the token. The Identity header is how SIP carries the STIR signature. This lab does not print a sample token or a private key.

sections.h: SHAKEN, as the opened pages describe it
paragraphs: The Secure Telephone Identity Governance Authority page says the STI-GA works with the IETF STIR protocol, and that the ATIS-SIP Forum SHAKEN specification specifies a practical mechanism for authenticating calls. The page says attaching a digital signature will help consumers trust caller ID, and that ATIS works with the STI-GA Board on rules for the certificate management infrastructure.

On the STI-GA page, SHAKEN is written out as Signature-based Handling of Asserted information using toKENs. The page says attaching a digital signature will help consumers trust caller ID, and that ATIS works with the STI-GA Board on rules for the certificate management infrastructure. This environment could not open the FCC call-authentication page, so this lesson does not repeat a deadline or a provider duty from that page. If the sources block shows confirm and no URL, open the page yourself. This is not legal advice.

lessons.title: Kari's Law, RAY BAUM'S Act, and SIP location
lessons.summary: Public Law 115-127 requires direct 911 dialing from MLTS. Section 506 of RAY BAUM'S Act requires a proceeding on dispatchable location. Educational only. Not legal advice.
objectives: State Kari's Law from the public law
State the section 506 duty as a proceeding, and the statutory definition
Keep RFC 6881 and RFC 6442 in the protocol column

illustration.title: Documents, not a checklist of your building
illustration.caption: Dates below are the ones printed in the public laws this lab opened. This environment could not open the FCC MLTS page, so no implementation date from that page is listed.
rows: Feb. 16, 2018. Kari's Law Act of 2017. Direct 911 dialing from MLTS.
Division of Public Law 115-141. Short title printed in the act.
Proceeding so dispatchable location is conveyed, including from MLTS.
Street address plus room, floor, or similar information.
BCP for emergency calling. Not legal advice.

paragraphs: Public Law 115-127, enacted February 16, 2018, is the Kari's Law Act of 2017. Its stated purpose is to amend the Communications Act of 1934 so multi-line telephone systems have a configuration that permits users to directly initiate a call to 9-1-1 without dialing any additional digit, code, prefix, or post-fix.

RAY BAUM'S Act of 2018 is a division of Public Law 115-141. The act says it may be cited as the Repack Airwaves Yielding Better Access for Users of Modern Services Act of 2018 or RAY BAUM'S Act of 2018. Section 506 requires the Commission to conclude a proceeding, not later than 18 months after enactment, to consider adopting rules so that the dispatchable location is conveyed with a 9-1-1 call, regardless of the technological platform, including calls from multi-line telephone systems. The section defines dispatchable location as the street address of the calling party and additional information such as room number, floor number, or similar information necessary to adequately identify the location of the calling party.

cites.label: Kari's Law Act of 2017, Public Law 115-127
Public Law 115-141, RAY BAUM'S Act of 2018

sections.h: Protocol documents, and the FCC page
paragraphs: RFC 6881 is a best current practice for communications services in support of emergency calling. It is not a statute. RFC 6442 defines a SIP extension to convey geographic location, including location-based routing. A SIP header that carries location is the protocol mechanism. It does not, by itself, prove a dispatchable location as the statute defines that term.

RFC 6881 is a best current practice. It does not replace the statute. This environment could not open the FCC MLTS page, so this lesson does not repeat an implementation date from that page. Read 47 CFR and the statute yourself. This lesson is not legal advice and not a determination about any system. If the sources block shows confirm and no URL, that is the FCC link.

cites.label: Kari's Law Act of 2017, Public Law 115-127

lessons.title: 10DLC is a messaging channel
lessons.summary: The Campaign Registry describes 10DLC as an A2P messaging channel with verified brands and campaign service providers. It is not SIP. Educational only.
objectives: Say what 10DLC is on the opened registry page
Keep it out of the SIP dialog
Refuse to invent a statute this lab did not open

illustration.title: Voice SIP versus the messaging registry
illustration.caption: If a vendor also sells both, the documents are still different.
rows: Brands and CSPs, on that page
Not a SIP header in RFC 3261
What the page says is given to the connectivity partner

paragraphs: The Campaign Registry home page says it is the backbone support for the 10DLC messaging ecosystem. It says 10DLC is an A2P messaging channel in which brands and campaign service providers are verified before they are allowed to send messages. It says campaigns can be registered through the CSP portal or APIs, and that messages are sent after the user gives their connectivity partner a Campaign ID.

The page also says to be a CSP before registering. This lab did not open a statute that uses the word 10DLC, so it does not claim a section number for one. Telephone consumer rules may still apply to messaging. Read those texts. This is not legal advice.

sections.h: What not to configure in the SIP proxy
paragraphs: A SIP INVITE does not become a 10DLC campaign because the From user looks like a telephone number. Kamailio, Asterisk, and FreeSWITCH are not named on the registry page this lab opened. Do not add a Campaign ID header to a voice INVITE and call it compliance.

When a design includes both voice SIP and application messaging, draw two paths. The voice path uses the SIP and RTP documents in the earlier tracks. The messaging path uses the registry and the carrier's current messaging rules. Mixing the traces wastes a troubleshooting hour.

paragraphs: A troubleshooting hour goes wrong when one symptom is asked to explain three regimes. No audio is a media problem: SDP, ICE, DTLS-SRTP, or the RTP proxy. A rejected caller ID story is an identity problem: RFC 8224, RFC 8225, and the SHAKEN governance page. A phone that cannot dial 911 without a prefix is the Kari's Law configuration, which is a statute and the FCC rules, not a codec.

An SMS campaign that will not send is The Campaign Registry's topic, plus whatever carrier rule you open. It will not show up as a missing a=rtpmap line. Write the next action as the name of the document and the observation, and stop before you declare the system compliant.

cites.label: Kari's Law Act of 2017, Public Law 115-127

sections.h: What a careful note looks like
paragraphs: A careful note says which message was seen, which document was opened, and what is still unknown. Example: INVITE left the PBX with no Identity header. RFC 8224 defines that header. This note does not say whether a rule required the header on this call.

For emergency tests, use the provider's test procedure. Do not place a live 911 call to satisfy this lesson. RFC 6881 remains a best current practice for how IETF protocols support emergency calling. It does not replace section 506 or the FCC rules. If a vendor debug guide disagrees with the statute, the statute is the law and the debug guide is the vendor's instructions. This is not legal advice.

quiz.q: No audio on a browser call is first
choices: A media problem: SDP, ICE, DTLS-SRTP
quiz.why: SHAKEN does not repair a missing DTLS handshake.

quiz.q: A required 9 before 911 is first
choices: The direct-dial statute and the FCC MLTS rules
quiz.why: Public Law 115-127 is the statute this lab opened.

cite.label: Kari's Law Act of 2017, Public Law 115-127

quiz.q: A missing Identity header is first
choices: RFC 8224, then the SHAKEN process you are actually in
quiz.why: Do not jump to a legal conclusion from the missing header alone.

quiz.q: Blocked A2P SMS is first
choices: The Campaign Registry and the carrier's messaging rules
quiz.why: It is not a SIP codec failure.

quiz.q: This lesson allows a live 911 call
choices: No. Use the provider's test procedure.
quiz.why: The study flow says not to place that call.

quiz.q: A careful note includes
choices: The observation, the document, and what is still unknown
The word compliant and nothing else
quiz.why: Unknowns stay written down.

cards.back: SIP, media, identity, location, or messaging.
Use the provider test. This lab is not that test.
RFC 8224. Presence is not a legal conclusion.
Counsel and the current rule outrank the quiz.

lab.title: Pick the next document
lab.prompt: One symptom. One next document. No legal conclusion.

check.q: Symptom: SMS from a new brand never leaves. The SIP phone works. Next document?
check.why: Working SIP does not debug an A2P messaging block.

fault.title: One-way audio blamed on SHAKEN
fault.symptom: The caller hears silence. Identity is present. The ticket says to rotate the STIR certificate.
choices: 10.1.2.3 in c= is a media reachability problem. Identity does not move RTP.
A certificate rotation repairs a private c= line
Silence means the PASSporT clock is 8000
fault.why: RTP follows the address in SDP. STIR is a signature on the request.
fault.cause: An identity feature was blamed for an unreachable media address.
fault.fix: Fix the media address or the anchor. Check the Identity header only if the symptom is caller identity.
